messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.content:
The standard error (i.e., the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under the null hypothesis) is

\[
SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{1.4}{\sqrt{40}} \approx \frac{1.4}{6.3249} \approx 0.221.
\]

So the null‑hypothesis test has a standard deviation of roughly **0.22**.
message.reasoning:
The user says: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6."

They want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test? That likely refers to the standard error of the mean under null hypothesis? The standard error = sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size). But they mention population mean 98.6. The standard deviation of the null hypothesis test might be the standard error of the difference between sample mean and population mean? Actually, the standard error of the sample mean is s / sqrt(n). So compute 1.4 / sqrt(40). sqrt(40) ≈ 6.3249. 1.4 / 6.3249 ≈ 0.2213. So standard error ~0.221.

But maybe they want the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the test statistic? For a t-test, the standard deviation of the null distribution of the t-statistic is sqrt((n-1)/(n-2))? No, that's not typical. Usually, the t-statistic has a t-distribution with df = n-1. The standard deviation of a t-distribution with df > 2 is sqrt(df/(df-2)). For df=39, sqrt(39/37) ≈ sqrt(1.0541) ≈ 1.0268. But the question: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6." They might want the standard error of the mean difference: sqrt((s^2/n) + (sigma^2/N))? But population mean is known, so we don't need population variance. The standard error of the difference between sample mean and population mean is s / sqrt(n). So answer ~0.221.

Alternatively, they might want the standard deviation of the null distribution of the test statistic: sqrt((n-1)/(n-2)). But that seems too advanced.

Given typical context, I'd answer: Standard error = 1.4 / sqrt(40) ≈ 0.221. So the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test is about 0.221.

Thus answer: Approximately 0.221.
